Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) election promise to ensure that Canada would be self-sufficient in energy by 1990 will not be kept, and that starting in 1987, Canada will have to import nearly one-half million barrels of oil per day; whereas the budget deficit for each of the two past years has been $3 billion, in other words almost 30 per cent more than what it would have been under a Progressive Conservative government; whereas the Right Hon. subsubtopic: TAXABLE EMPLOYEE BENEFITS-REQUEST THAT MINISTER REVIEW BUDGET MEASURE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Despite assurances to the contrary from the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism, the effect of the combined increase in taxable benefits for employees is not offset by the lower marginal tax rate. Figures show that the budget measures concerning taxable employee benefits have a progressively negative impact on employees earning less than $40,000. The lower and middle-income wage earners in the work force are the ones who are feeling the impact. Would the Minister of Finance give serious review to the taxable benefit issue in his budget and bring this measure into line with his stated objective of equity and fairness?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: TAXABLE EMPLOYEE BENEFITS-REQUEST THAT MINISTER REVIEW BUDGET MEASURE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I believe the comments made by the Minister of State are fully justified. The total new liability on taxpayers as a result of the tax on these benefits in the range, for example, of the average industrial wage in Canada, is more than offset by the other tax benefits flowing from the budget, and I believe when we get into committee we will be able to demonstrate that to the satisfaction of the hon. member.

Madam Speaker, the average industrial wage has nothing to do with the fairness and
equity I am talking about with regard to employees who need their taxable benefits.
It will take a pay increase of at least 4 per cent to maintain the pre-November 12 spending power of employees affected by the taxable benefit rules in the minister's budget. At a time when the Prime Minister is asking us to restrain wages and tighten our belts, the Minister of Finance is forcing employees to demand more from employers. Will the Minister of Finance remove this inflationary and counterproductive measure which hits employees least able to afford it?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as hon. members are aware, the review and scrutiny by Parliament of the government's expenditure plans is one of the fundamental responsibilities of the parliamentary system. Thus, as the plans which are being tabled, and for which authorization is requested, are within the expenditure framework tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in his budget of November 12, I invite all hon. members to devote their efforts to a full and complete examination of these estimates.
Before highlighting some of the content of this year's estimates I would like to say a few words about the presentation itself.
Last year this government tabled for the first time a Part I to the estimates to provide hon. members with a context for reviewing the estimates, or Blue Book, which contains both the statutory expenditures and the voted items for which parliamentary authority is sought for expenditures to be incurred during the coming fiscal year. It has been agreed by all concerned, I believe, that Part I serves a very useful purpose as it allows for an explanation of forward multiyear plans which could not be incorporated in the Blue Book, and provides a variety of analysis and explanation in a form which is more easily assimilated than that of the formal estimates.
I am tabling Part I, the government expenditure plan, again this year. This volume shows the five-year expenditure plan of the government, including the breakdown by ten "spending envelopes". In addition, considerable analysis and explanation is provided to give members a better understanding of the content of the plan and the 1982-83 estimates.

Further, as part of my project to improve reporting to parliament, 1 am pleased to table, on behalf of the responsible ministers, ten program expenditure plans, or separate volumes of a new Part III of the Estimates. Members will recall that it was my intention to table nine such plans this year, but in fact ten are available. This is the first time that these program
Main Estimates, 1982-83
expenditure plans have been tabled with the Main Estimates, although last year I tabled a number of pilot projects based on the Estimates for 1980-81, simply to serve as examples and to invite comment from members. The purpose of the Part III booklets is to provide members with a much more detailed explanation of the management plans and systems of individual departments than is presented in the Blue Book. These program expenditure plans are prepared by and are the responsibility of the individual departments and are intended to provide members with additional assistance in their scrutiny of individual programs. The tables repeated in these volumes from the Blue Book have been verified by the Treasury Board Secretariat. I am working to a schedule which will see all departments submit their expenditure plans for the year 198586; in the interim, there will be an increase in the number tabled each year.
There has been considerable discussion in this House and in committees of the difficulties that members have in understanding the expenditure proposals of the government through reviews of the content of the Blue Book. As a former member of the Public Accounts Committee, I fully appreciate the problems involved. The Public Accounts Committee has conducted a thorough review of the government's proposals on the Estimates. As well, discussions on these documents took place with some 25 individual Members of Parliament. The recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee and the members have resulted in a number of changes to enable these expenditure plans to better meet Parliament's needs. In addition to these consultations and recommendations three distinguished former parliamentarians, the Hon. Otto Lang, James Gillies and Douglas Fisher, were invited to review last year's pilot projects and to offer their comments. I am most grateful for their co-opeiation. I would also like to thank all members of the House and others who have made such a constructive contribution to the development of these departmental expenditure plans. The tabling of the first ten plans today is indeed a landmark in the evolution of the accountability of government to Parliament, and as members will know, in keeping with the recommendations of the Lambert commission and the Auditor General, as well as the Public Accounts Committee itself. I believe that these program expenditure plans go far toward fulfilling the information needs of Parliament. As a cautionary point, it is also important that Members of Parliament recognize that additional improvements in the expenditure plans will occur over time. This is a major undertaking by individual departments, and thus will be developed over the next few years as underlying information systems and procedures are expanded or improved.
In the context of our consultation with hon. members, other options were explored for providing additional assistance in

reviewing the estimates. Therefore, today I have also made available to hon. members a short "Guide to the Estimates". This document explains the nature of the current revisions to the estimates and briefly outlines the manner in which hon. members can obtain information through the various estimates documents.
I do want to emphasize the importance which this government attaches to the project being managed by the Comptroller General to improve the presentation of estimates to Parliament. This will help each and every hon. member of this House to carry out his or her fundamental and democratic responsibility of ensuring that taxes paid by Canadians will be used for the benefit of all Canadians. The preparation and tabling of Part I and a further stage of Part III, plus the "Guide to the Estimates", I believe, is tangible evidence of the effort this government is making to facilitate the carrying out of our parliamentary responsibilities. Our purpose is to provide full disclosure and to encourage rigorous scrutiny by all hon. members on behalf of the people of Canada.
I would now like to describe certain specific aspects of the information in these documents. First of all, may I point out that the updated expenditure plan to 1985-86, set out in Part I of the estimates, provides for the same total spending level in 1982-83 and future years as was envisaged by my colleague the Minister of Finance when he tabled his budget on November 12 last year. In other words, the estimates are entirely compatible with the information tabled by the Minister of Finance. The numbers set forth in the estimates are destined and designed to proceed upon the presumptions underlying that budget.
I would like to draw the attention of hon. members to two adjustments which must be made in reconciling the total estimates to the planned total spending level of $76.3 billion as set forth in the material of the Minister of Finance; that is to say, as set forth in the budget.
First, total estimates must be adjusted downward for repayment of loans from previous years which are not offset by new loans. The current estimate of these repayments is $480 million.
Second, since the government cannot legally spend more money than Parliament authorizes, and in fact always spends less, an adjustment for this lapse of expenditure authority must be made. The current projection of the lapse for the year 198283 is $1.23 billion.

I wish to emphasize to members that the expenditure plan reflects our intention to continue imposing a high degree of restraint on spending for the currently approved programs of the government. While recognizing the difficulties involved in making precise forecasts of costs for more than a year ahead, the Treasury Board's most recent review tends to indicate that it will take careful planning and determined management by all ministers and departments to carry out the operations of government within the limits of these envelopes. My colleagues
are aware of the need for continued prudence and restraint in light of the particular difficulties and uncertainties facing us in the planning years beyond 1982-83.
And now, Madam Speaker, I would like to comment on the result of the $100 million reduction in overhead expenses of the government which was included as an item in the November budget. As part of the review leading up to these Main Estimates, every program of government was required to substantiate the price increases it has experienced over the past year. In many cases, these numbers were based on actual invoices or contracts for the provision of goods and services. However, it was felt that the operating costs of government should not be fully protected from the effects of inflation, and as a result, the price increases included in these Estimates have been substantially reduced from the levels that would otherwise have been allocated to departments. These reductions were applied to virtually all programs of government in order to effect savings in areas such as transportation and communication expenditures and in the purchase of materials and supplies. While these savings may not be significant in terms of total government spending, they are substantial in relation to those expenditures related to the overhead of government and reflect one additional measure in the continued struggle for efficiency and restraint.

The creation of the Canada Post Corporation has also had a significant impact on the level of resources that are being requested in the 1982-83 Main Estimates. As a department, the post office required appropriations in order to finance all of its operating and capital requirements with most of its revenue not being used to offset its expenditures. The 1981-82 Main Estimates included over $1.7 billion for this purpose. The government is only required to provide for Canada Post's net operating deficit, now that it is a Crown corporation and retains the postal revenues, and consequently no appropriation requirements are included in the 1982-83 Main Estimates. However, the total spending levels for 1982-83 included in the budget have a provision for a $400 million deficit, and Parliament will be asked to approve an item for this purpose through a supplementary estimate in 1982-83.
The comparisons between fiscal years included in Part I of the estimates have been adjusted to treat Canada Post as if it had always been a Crown corporation. The conversion to a Crown corporation has also had an effect on other aspects of the Main Estimates. As a Crown corporation, Canada Post is now required to pay for certain services which were previously provided without charge by other departments and, conversely, departmental appropriations must now include provision for services provided by the new corporation. The most significant example of this arrangement is the inclusion of $220 million in the arts and culture program of the Department of Communications for postal subsidies on cultural-related mailings that were previously calculated as part of the operating requirements of the old post office department.

In addition, the size of the public service has come to be measured by the number of person-years subject to Treasury Board control, and with the conversion to Crown corporation status the person-years of Canada Post are no longer considered in this category.
1 would like to turn for a moment to this question of person-years. After making the adjustment for Canada Post and another similar technical modification, I am once again pleased to announce that, despite the continued pressure in the system for the provision of more and more services, growth in the size of the public service has been kept to less than 1 per cent. The 1982-83 Main Estimates provide for 255,322 person-years, which represents an increase of 2,152 or .8 per cent over the comparable figure for 1981-82.
[ Translation]
One important perspective related to the growth in person-years that is often overlooked involves the fact that many of the government's services provided to the public are actually cost-recovered. The total direct costs associated with over 19,000 person-years are completely paid for by fees and charges resulting from activities provided to the public. Obviously, increased resources, including person-years, for services that are essentially cost-recoverable, should be treated differently from those that merely increase the general overhead of the government. In fact, a significant portion of some of the largest cost increases over the 1981-82 levels is recovered through the provision of services. Many of the 434 additional person-years for the RCMP will be used for policing at the detachment level which is recoverable through the recently renegotiated contracts with the provinces and municipalities. In the Department of Transport, almost one half of its total increase of 375 person-years will be used for air traffic control and systems that derive revenues from various sources related to the use of airports and Canada's airways.
It should also be pointed out that all operating and personnel costs are recovered for a further 20,000 person-years related to the administration of the Unemployment Insurance and the Canada Pension Plan programs.

Finally, I would like to point out that the 1982-83 Main Estimates do not reflect the recently announced reorganization which primarily affected the Departments of Industry, Trade and Commerce, Regional Economic Expansion and External Affairs. Quite simply, there has not been sufficient time to work out all of the adjustments that will be necessary. Once the details of the resource reallocations of the new department of regional industrial expansion, the enlarged responsibilities for External Affairs and the other adjustments have been finalized. Parliament will then be provided with an opportunity to review these proposals through a special 1982-83 supplementary estimate.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is a very interesting day. I want to delve back into history just a little bit, if I might. The last estimates that were presented in this House of Commons by the Diefenbaker government in 1963 totalled $7 billion. At the beginning of the reign of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the estimates, which I have here in this little slim volume for 1968-69, totalled only $12.4 billion.
The estimates that we are dealing with today for the year 1982-83 which come in this large volume, which takes a healthy, well-fit man to carry around for more than twice the length of the Parliament Buildings, and that includes me, amount in total to $74.2 billion. That is a 500 per cent increase in government expenditures in that period of time, or an increase of approximately six times.
That ought to strike fear into the hearts of those who look at the state of the economy, the height of the interest rates and a host of other things in considering the government's record. The only people who can feel joyful and happy about that kind of increase are those who do not fear continuous government intervention in the economy. I would be the last to suggest that it could cease, but I would be the first to suggest that there has not been the appropriate watch placed on it, the pragmatic approach to government. As time goes on, given the policies of this government, I think one will see the continuation of that kind of increase in an equally short period of time.
I would like to pay tribute to my friend, the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens). It was the hon. member for York-Peel who, when he was president of the Treasury Board during the Clark government, brought into play in terms of government expenditures the envelope system for expenditure. It was something quite new in terms of expenditures.
What that system managed to do was to place responsibility for finding the wherewithal to fund government programs on ministers and departments which came up with those programs. That is putting it very simply, but I think very clearly. 1 am very pleased to see that that system is being carried on by the present government because it is sound. It is important that the public know where it began. It did not begin with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) who has just finished speaking. It began under the leadership in Treasury Board of the hon. member for York-Peel.
The second point that is important to remember is that all of these programs, the program expenditure plans of government, those ten programs which the President of Treasury Board referred to, came out of the work of the Public Accounts
February 23, 1982

Committee, chaired from time to time by members of the opposition parties. It was chaired for a period of time by the President of the Treasury Board, the member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), the member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) and a host of other people who brought forward those plans, drawing upon the learning and experience of Mr. Lambert and the fresh view of controlling expenditures which he and others like him have brought into government.
I am concerned about one aspect of the minister's statement, and I think it important that we set the record straight. If one takes the minister's statement, which 1 have in front of me, at face value, he said at page three:
Based on the assumptions of the November budget, total forecast spending of $76.3 billion in 1982-83 is 11.7 per cent higher than the forecast for 1981 -82.
That is dealing with forecasts, Madam Speaker. Those forecasts are wrong. In fact, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has refused to table forecasts or give any credence to forecasts-even the ones he has given in his own budget.
If anyone in the country believes that the total government expenditure in Canada will increase by only 11.7 per cent from the previous year, I suggest that they are wrong. The only solid basis on which to chart the increase in government expenditures is to go from Main Estimates to Main Estimates. If we take the figures from the Main Estimates we have just seen and relate them to the Main Estimates for the previous year, we find that the government expenditures in that area do not increase by only 11.7 per cent, they increase by 15 per cent. That is the first statement I would like to make.
The second matter I would like to point out is that from time to time the government has said that it would keep its rate of increase in government spending below the rate of inflation. That has not happened because although the rate of inflation is high enough in Canada, it is not 15 per cent. In that respect the estimates which have been tabled today do not fall within the content of former statements or statements of purpose. They fall by the wayside like so many other statements made by this government.
I will deal briefly with some items which I think people should know about. First is the item of advertising. The advertising program is up by 14 per cent from the previous year. It amounts to approximately $70 million. There is $1 billion yet to come in supplementary estimates to be tabled some time in March. Salaries and wages for public servants will have to be examined very closely because the numbers do not coincide with existing contracts or probable inflation. After adjusting for the post office changes, the total salaries from last year's Main Estimates to this year's Main Estimates are up only by 7 per cent in spite of an increase in the size of the public service. These figures do not add up. Inquiries will have to be made into that aspect.
According to these estimates, public debt charges are up by 14 per cent this year. Government borrowing accounted for 44 per cent of the money raised in the financial markets last year.
Main Estimates 1982-83
Imagine the impact on interest rates if the government would reduce its level of borrowing. Can you imagine that impact, Madam Speaker, and what it would mean for home owners and small business people?
There has been no change in the estimated cost of servicing the public debt since the November budget. The government surely must know by now that its revenues will be less than it expects which will result in a larger debt and a larger debt service cost.
The figure for equalization in the estimates reveals quite a substantial increase over the 1981-82 figure. However, during today's briefing government officials told our officials that this represented a continuation of the existing formula, not the new Ontario standard which was proposed in the budget or the five provinces standard which was proposed during the first ministers' meetings. Also, the estimates for transfers to the provinces do not take into account the census estimates of revised population which may result in pay-backs for previous years for some provinces to Ottawa. So it becomes evident that there are many concerns.
I would like to remind the House of what Ray Buxton, President of the Canadian Real Estate Association, said in a statement on February 15 about the size of the government's borrowing and its impact upon interest rates. He said:
The federal government could open the gates to more widespread home ownership if it reduced its heavy borrowings.
He estimated that this would reduce interest rates by 1 'A per cent to 2 per cent:
-thereby increasing the number of families who would qualify for mortgages.
There is nothing in the estimates, Madam Speaker, to attack the great problem of housing in Canada.
I do not want to be unkind to the minister but I do want to be truthful with him. There is a great deal of skepticism in Canada about the ability, and indeed the will, of the government to control its expenditures and act in a businesslike fashion. Recently the member for York-Peel brought a document to the public's attention which detailed improvidence in the government in the great computer caper. Improvidence in the government, Madam Speaker. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Gray) said that the government learned a lesson. They sure did and we sure paid for that lesson!
If we review the estimates, we see that the estimated cost of the Guy Favreau project in Montreal has jumped from $44 million to $83 million. Perhaps the President of the Treasury Board can indicate why there is such a leap. There has been a history of understating and overstating the estimates and the truth with regard to estimating programs, which has been, as far as Canadians are concerned, something completely different from the statement by the minister, whatever sugary language he manages to use.
You will remember that I raised in the House the report of the Auditor General. His report indicated that the net debt of the government is understated by $9 billion. For the first time in Canada's history there had to be a qualified certificate on

February 23, 1982
Main Estimates 1982-83
the operations of the Canadian government. That is why we are somewhat skeptical about these pronouncements.
There have been some incredible examples revealed to us about the government's inability to manage the public's money. 1 have a couple of examples to illustrate our skepticism and wonder about these estimates, which make us want to examine them very, very closely. For example, there was $110,000 paid for metric cooking lessons. Two television chefs, Bruno Gerussi and Madame Benoit, have been given a six-week television contract worth $110,000 to promote metric cooking.
There is the case of interest free loans to Michael Phelps, the executive assistant to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). Fie has received two interest-free mortgages from Petro-Canada totalling $35,000. At current interest rates, the annual cost of these mortgages to taxpayers would be in the range of $6,000 to $7,000, even if they are justified or authorized in the first place. Another example are the cost overruns at Place du Portage, the C.D. Howe Building and the Montreal postal plant.
Do hon. members remember the JetStars? This is what makes me wonder about the government's honest intention to control expenditures.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Madam Speaker. I appreciate your consideration.
This minister is the same minister who is charged with the responsibility of bringing in legislation with respect to Crown corporations and accountability. The House has not seen that
legislation yet. Two years ago the minister said he would be the master of regulatory reform. We have not seen any processes for regulatory reform. I know regulatory reform is being worked at by the bureaucracy, but it is not out here in public.
This is the government which two years ago said it was committed to openness of government so that people would know. Freedom of information was the watchword. Just a few days ago the round-heeled Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) was blown over by a blast of wind from the attorneys general. We are not likely to see freedom of information.
Let us look at the unanswered questions on the Order Paper with respect to government expenditures. The whole process of accountability will not work if it is the view of the government that the senior people in Crown corporations will not even have their salaries revealed. How can we judge their accountability? These are the things Mr. Lambert talked about, and if we are going to close the ring on expenditure management in government, we have to have some parliamentary reform. That was another watchword of the government two years ago, but there has not been one proposal.
When the minister is musing over the Blue Book, as thick as it has become, he should reread the last section of the Lambert report, which talks about improving the processes in Parliament so that the people of Canada, through their elected representatives, can find out what goes on within government. Until that is done no member of this House of Commons ought to be content with bland statements by the government or mere changes in the Blue Book process, as far-reaching as they are.
1 urge the President of the Treasury Board to do his duty, light a fire under the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) and get him going, because we have a long way to go in order to complete the ring of accountability Mr. Lambert spoke about in his report.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to respond on behalf of the New Democratic Party as our Treasury Board critic and as a member of the Public Accounts Committee.
The revised form of the estimates has changed the package quite substantially since I became a Member of Parliament some two years ago. Originally the Blue Book was a very difficult document to understand. It was difficult for the Parliament of Canada to get a grasp on accountability for expenditures by the government, and I would like to compliment the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) and the office of the Comptroller General for making this package of documents much more understandable. It is now easier to get a grip on the expenditures of government or at least what its plans are.
I would not want the government to be satisfied with that, however. There are other improvements I think need to be made. An example which comes to mind is that the information on the plans and objectives of the government and the objectives of the different departments, the Blue Book and the
February 23, 1982

guide with which to use it which make up the four parts of the revised form of estimates, must be consistent with the public accounts at the end of the year so that we can actually compare the results of the year's spending with the projections put out in the revised form of the estimates.
In talking about the estimates this year I have some confusion yet as to what the actual amount of the expenditures have been. According to fact sheet No. 1:
Total forecast spending of $76.3 billion in 1982-83 is 11.7 per cent higher than the forecast for 1981-82.
According to fact sheet No. 4:
The 1982-83 Main Estimates tabled today provide for $72,935 million in budgetary expenditures, an increase of $9,503 million or 15 per cent over the 1981-82 Main Estimates.
I suppose in terms of actual dollars, we are talking only about $4 billion, which may not be much in terms of federal government expenditures, but many Members of Parliament have a hard time grasping what is actually happening when there are contradictions like that. The information has to flow in a way which is a bit more fluid and consistent than has been the case up to this point in time.
As I say, progress has been made by the office of the Comptroller General under the direction of the President of the Treasury Board. It has been good up until now, but it must continue.
I am very concerned about the amount of spending which is being undertaken to service the public debt. The public debt accounts for some 23 per cent of the total expenditures placed before us today, and that is a phenomenal amount of money. I think about one dollar of every five raised in revenue goes back to servicing the public debt. I think repayment of the public debt is of great importance to Members of Parliament, but the government goes about the repayment of that debt in a strange way. 1 am concerned that responsibility for that public debt is being placed on the backs of provincial and municipal governments.
The total accumulated public debt brought about by this government is now about $81 billion, and this government is going to address the reduction of that debt by transferring certain responsibilities to provincial and municipal governments. Established programs financing comes to mind. Over the next five years those transfers to the provinces will be reduced by some $5.7 billion. There is evidence of the transfer of that responsibility. The community services contribution program was cut some 18 months ago, and that created a real hardship for many municipal governments across the country. With respect to policing costs, a heavier burden was placed on provincial and municipal governments, and that put the federal government in a better-looking financial position. Another part of this is that the federal government is trying to get away from statutory payments associated with the Crow rate.
The situation in relation to person-years is somewhat deceiving. The reduction of federal government person-years appears to be large. Some 60,000 or more jobs have been removed from the authority of the Treasury Board and transferred to Crown corporations, and this raises the very serious
Main Estimates 1982-83
point to which the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) referred. There is a need for a Crown corporations act because more and more responsibility is being transferred from the authority of Parliament, and even away from the authority of the government to some extent. That responsibility is being assumed by Crown corporations. As a member of the Public Accounts Committee, the last I heard was that there were some 464 federal Crown corporations under the four different schedules A, B, C and D. This number is growing all the time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: We do not know how many there are.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
I suppose some of these might be called agencies which are set up in such a way that the federal government is a shareholder, but these agencies do not appear as Crown corporations and there is a real need for a Crown corporations act. We must establish whether Crown corporations are instruments of public policy. Do they reflect the wishes of the government and the wishes of Parliament, and how do we as parliamentarians scrutinize the activities of a large number of federal Crown corporations? More are being created all the time. Two new Crown corporations are being formed for the post office and the museums. It has been announced that $185 million will be spent on creating two new museums in order that artifacts which are presently deteriorating can be preserved. In fact, some reporters have called the museums a national disgrace.
I would not want to make a judgment on whether Crown corporations will be good or bad; time will tell. They will certainly not be accountable to the public, however, if the government keeps on the course it is embarked upon now.
I was shocked when the new chief executive officer of Canada Post appeared before the Standing Committee on Public Accounts at a time when the Auditor General was also present. Testimony revealed that the Auditor General, along with a private firm, will be co-auditor of that particular Crown corporation for a two-year period. It also came out in evidence that a letter had been sent to the Auditor General by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I am paraphrasing somewhat but it was to the effect that the Auditor General should not expect to be reappointed as co-auditor to Canada Post when his two-year appointment expires.
I think that demonstrates that the government is interfering in the responsibility that parliamentarians have toward the great expenditures made on behalf of the Canadian taxpayer. There is provision for scrutiny of such expenditure by a Crown corporation. It makes the person-years of the government look good and it makes government expenditures look good, but we as parliamentarians do not know what is happening in many of the Crown corporations. We do not know whether they are instruments of public policy or whether they are embarked upon some course of their own. They may be doing a good job but then they may not, and we do not have access to the information that would allow us to make that judgment.

February 23, 1982
Main Estimates 1982-83
1 urge the President of the Treasury Board to address the problem of the accessibility of information from Crown corporations. There should be an improvement in the amount of information that is available to parliamentarians so that they do not have to wrestle with the estimates, although 1 do agree that the package has been improved. The expenditure plans submitted by each department will be a great help. Until now opposition critics for certain departments or agencies of government only had the Blue Book to go by, but now an analysis is submitted by each department of its ojectives and goals for the coming year. That information will be very useful to the critics in the official opposition and in the New Democratic Party.
I would ask the President of the Treasury Board to consider well the comments and recommendations made by Members of Parliament. 1 hope that in days to come we will not be deceived by the information we receive. Perhaps I can hope for a Crown corporations act so that the Auditor General, who is really an officer of Parliament, can act on our behalf and give us information on money being spent out of the public purse. I do not believe we have full control of the public purse yet but the more information we have, the better chance we have of getting it under control.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wonder if the minister is aware that questions about government expenditures on advertising have been on the Order Paper in my name for over a year and a half. To date they have not been answered. advertising budget, the information was promised but has not been forthcoming. If we cannot get it in that context, then will the President of the Treasury Board undertake to provide Parliament with the information that is requested?

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister about another aspect of his responsibilities. My colleague, the critic for Treasury Board, noted that for two years the minister has been incapable of coming to Parliament for legislation to improve the financial control and accountability of Crown corporations, notwithstanding the fact that in the brief nine months the Clark government was in office such legislation was tabled in the House. On numerous occasions the minister had indicated that he intended to take urgent action to present such legislas-tion to Parliament. This relates directly to his responsibility and to control of expenditures in the estimates for those Crown corporations. Can he tell the House why he has failed so dismally to keep the commitment that he made to the House, and will he indicate when he will keep it?

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's interest in Crown corporations. I share with him and with all hon. members a concern about the accountability of what has grown to be a very large part of the public sector. Bill C-27 was tabled, as you will recall. I have stated in the House a number of times that it contained a number of defects which were pointed out by heads of Crown corporations, officials in departments, people outside government, the audit community and others. As a result, we have undertaken a very extensive review of the legislation with a view to better achieving accountability, direction and control of Crown corporations.
Because of the assets involved, however, and because of the ongoing impact of this legislation or the reorganization that we may introduce to accomplish the specific purposes which I am sure we all share, I have not been able to put every matter to rest. I can assure the hon. member, however, that a great deal of progress has been made and I hope that in the near term action will be taken with respect to the whole area of control, direction and accountability of Crown corporations. 1 know this matter is of great concern to him, as it is to me.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is two years since the minister was appointed and he has given those assurances on several occasions during the time. I wonder if he could give us a time frame today-to the nearest month even-on when he will introduce that legislation.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, usually the hon. member's information, via brown envelopes or otherwise, is somewhat more accurate than the ridiculous declaration he has made to the House. The project is far from dead. It is one of continuing and great concern to the Prime Minister. After all, back in 1976 it was the Privy Council that developed what 1 believe was called the blue paper at that time with respect to Crown corporations. Everything I have said in the past stands; the commitments stand, the concern stands and action is being taken.
I would expect hon. members to recognize, however, that this House has had a fairly heavily charged scheduled of activity in the past year that I have been in this portfolio. That does not detract in any way from the importance of the Crown corporation legislation. Great progress had been made and I hope that when action is taken I will have the full co-operation of the hon. member to put through the House the legislation that is necessary to establish the direction, accountability and control that we all want.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, let me in my last question ask the minister, if he will not pin it down to the nearest month, whether he will commit himself to the House to introduce that legislation before summer. subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, commitments can only be as effective as is the House in dealing with legislation when it is brought down. The most I can say to the hon. member today is that I am anxious to proceed with this matter as soon as possible. If it is within a month I would be delighted; if it is within several months I would still be delighted. I certainly hope it is within the time frame of which the hon. member is speaking, but I refuse to stand in the House at this point to say that we will have this legislation by June 1, July 1 or April 1. The fact is that we are moving ahead steadily with it, and I hope to have further announcements to make in the very near term.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have great difficulty understanding how a minister can rise in his place and give an answer such as the one the President of the Treasury Board just gave respecting a matter which has been outstanding for two years.
Also the government indicated that it is generally in favour of the report of the Lambert commission on accountability of government. In that report there are provisions whereby Mr. Lambert and his colleagues recommended that committees of the House of Commons have tabled before them on an automatic basis the reports of all Crown corporations, agencies and
Main Estimates 1982-83
departments of government, that they be given complete scope in order to examine the operations of government, and that it would be an appropriate arrangement for parliamentary reform.
As the minister responsible for the Lambert report, what is his view with respect to that provision? Madam Speaker, let me clarify my mandate. I am the minister responsible for co-ordinating the government's response to the report of the Lambert commission. I have already tabled in the House a publication entitled "Accountable Management", with respect to which I received some very complimentary comments from the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, for which I thank him. I know he recognizes that we have made enormous progress in a wide variety of areas across government in achieving the kind of accountability which Mr. Lambert and commission members suggested and recommended. We have also moved ahead in the personnel field or in the area of human resource management pursuant to the report of the D'Avignon Committee. All of this was pulled together in the publication "Accountable Management", with which the hon. member is familiar.
In addition, during my budget speech back in November I updated the House on where we were with respect to various outstanding issues concerning the responses to Lambert and D'Avignon. I agree with the hon. member that there is a further area which must be addressed. I look forward to hearing his contributions in the House with respect to the issue of parliamentary reform which is within the jurisdiction of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard). He and I have discussed the issue of parliamentary reform and will continue to discuss it. I believe the minister indicated the other day that he would be bringing forward some proposals and that he had already undertaken some discussions with the other House leaders respecting the question of parliamentary reform. I share the desire of the hon. member to close the loop of accountability which he mentioned earlier this afternoon.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have one further question. We are agreed that the programs examined in the course of our work are serving vital social needs and merit undiminished support. Over-all funding of these programs should, in our view, be maintained at no less than current levels.
Did the President of the Treasury Board take any of this information under advisement before giving approval to the estimates for this year and the coming year? It seems as if he has totally looked away from it.

With respect to established program financing, the estimates are designed to reflect the policy and financial requirements stated by the Minister of Finance when he tabled the budget on November 12, 1981. They are not for long-budgeted items such as the western development fund, so that smokescreen type of explanation does not follow the minister's officials' position.
I would like to know whether it is possible to move moneys into the western development fund. Is that the process, or is it just a mirage? Could he tell us exactly what the western development fund is since it was budgeted so long ago?

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is not much that I would add to the answers I have already given on the subject. Obviously there is a margin, there is a reserve, there are programs that will be tabled here in the House by our colleagues-I am here today to answer questions on the estimates. I have not mentioned the western development fund in my speech nor in my comments nor in the analysis 1 have given in the House today. I should like such questions to be put to my colleagues who are responsible for such matters.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have listened to my colleague the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) and the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) trying to find out about a matter which has been touted and promised by the Liberal government ever since the last Speech from the Throne. To then find out that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) does not even know what the western development fund is all about is a
matter which causes a lot of concern and chagrin to those of us in western Canada.
The only question I want to ask the minister is if he would confirm-this will, of course, get a great laugh across western Canada-that there is nothing in the current estimates dealing with the western development fund as such.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is not a question of confirming that there is nothing in the current estimates regarding that fund. The estimates are there for programs and for the ongoing operations of the government. They are divided into the voted programs and statutory programs. The Main Estimates are deposited to be referred to committee and will subsequently be the subject of an appropriation bill in this House. The hon. member will have ample opportunity to examine those programs in committee.
As I pointed out, the estimates are only part of the over-all expenditure plan which provides for reserves, for programs such as the western development fund, which programs, whatever the details may be, will be announced in due course by the responsible ministers. They will be the subject of supplementary estimates, and the hon. member, who has been in this House a great deal longer than 1 have, will then know that he can in turn go back to the responsible minister, examine him in committee, and in turn the programs will be the subject of further appropriation bills in this House.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
What concerns me, Madam Speaker, is that the last time the minister tabled the Main Estimates there was a provision for $350 million for the western development fund. That has evaporated. Yet we have had statements by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) that this in fact will be forthcoming and is a firm commitment of the government.
I would simply make the comment that the government has again failed western Canada and it is no wonder the Liberals are doing so poorly politically out there.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1982-83 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I can understand the hon. member playing politics when the President of the Treasury Board responds to questions on the estimates, but surely any objective assessment of the programs committed to during the last two years by this government to western Canada development is enough to allay the fears of any westerner that the government is not committed to western programs.

Were any studies done which established a scientific basis for the contention that an increase in marine mammal population would damage over-all fish production and, if so, what were the names and who were the authors of the studies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
A scientific consultation on marine mammals convened by the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Bergen, Norway in 1976 agreed that interactions of various kinds between marine mammals and fisheries were significantly affecting some sea fisheries; mostly adversely, apparently. A subsequent review of this matter by the IUCN interim committee on marine mammals led to the holding of a workshop on marine mammal/fishery interactions held at La Jolla, California in 1981.
This workshop, attended by eminent specialists from the U.S.A., Canada, Great Britain, Italy, Australia, Norway and the U.S.S.R., considered several aspects of the biotic and other interactions between marine mammals and fisheries, with emphasis on fisheries of commercial importance.
Studies and case histories considered under those aspects which would result in damage to over-all fish production are listed below:
Loss of fish production through damage to the catch, to gear, or through interference with the catching efficiency of fishing gear:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to raise a point of order concerning the answering of questions on the Order Paper. Some questions have been on the Order Paper for eight to ten months, with a great many having been there longer than six months. Some of them are quite simple and could be answered with little or no effort. It is obvious to me, in looking at the Order Paper, that there are a great many questions which the government has made no effort to obtain answers to. In my submission this can only be by deliberate intention since in the normal course they would be answered automatically.
My colleague the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) referred to the difficulty opposition members have in getting information out of the government. The hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) referred to his inability to get information from officials in committee and ministers in the House. The result is. Madam Speaker, that the practice of putting questions on the Order Paper is rapidly becoming a time consuming and rather pointless exercise. The fact is that there are close to 250 pages of unanswered questions on the Order Paper after a session which has gone on for more than 280 days. In fact, there has only been one session longer than this one. It is an indication and an indictment of the government's indifference and arrogance with regard to this institution and the rights and privileges of its members.
If the government, Madam Speaker, does not intend to answer questions on the Order Paper, such as the one the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) has had on for five years and God knows how many weeks and days, if it intends to treat Parliament with such indifference and contempt, then there is little point in putting questions on an Order Paper which grows every Monday.
In my submission, this is something, which hon. members will have to take under advisement. I am not quite sure what the government is trying to do here. Many Canadians are wondering about that. I know we are not here to go through futile exercises at the behest of a government which is in one of
its longest sessions on record and has very little to show for the time that it has spent.
1 make the point that if it is the government's policy not to answer questions on the Order Paper, or only to answer the ones with which it is comfortable and which will not embarrass it, then there is little or no point in carrying on with the practice. Perhaps it will be necessary that we have recourse through orders of the House for everything we get. These have already reached an unprecedented number of unfilled orders. If we continue in that way, we may have to seek an opinion from the House on this government's laxity and its contemp of the institution.
It is not surprising that a government which cannot bring down a budget cannot answer questions. That does not surprise me at all. The House is entitled to know whether or not this policy of inaction is a deliberate policy, whether it will continue, or whether hon. members can look forward to receiving answers within a reasonable time limit of a week or two instead of six or seven months or, indeed more than five years.
There was a time when hon. members could indicate the importance of a question by placing an asterisk beside it, a starred question. That practice has fallen into disuse, because it is being ignored by the government. Hon. members placed a star beside a question to indicate its urgency and to require an oral answer. At one time that was a respected practice of this House.
It does no good for the parliamentary secretary to tell us how well he has done in answering over 2,000 questions. The fact is that since this practice commenced, the number of hon. members of this House has substantially grown. That is one of the reasons more questions are being asked.
Another reason more questions are being asked is this government's obsession with secrecy and its resistance to providing information of any kind to hon. members. If this continues much longer, we in the opposition will have no recourse but to ask that Your Honour exercise your discretion in favour of upholding the rights of hon. members, and to entertain with favour a question of privilege which will have to be posed if we are to be continually refused by the governe-ment. The whole matter will have to be referred either to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, or to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, because the logjam must be broken. The government must change its attitude and adopt one of providing information to the people of Canada, through their representatives on all sides of this House, to which they are entitled.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the hon. member raises a question of privilege on this particular question, I will read a quotation from Beauchesne's fifth edition, Citation 363, whereby it is very clearly stated that in no way can the Chair oblige a minister to answer a question. That also applies, of course, to the questions on the Order Paper. Citation 363 states:
(I) A minister may decline to answer a question without stating the reason for his refusal, and insistence on an answer is out of order, with no debate being allowed. A refusal to answer cannot be raised as a question of privilege, nor is it regular to comment upon such a refusal. A member may put a question but has no right to insist upon an answer.
That is quite clear. Answers to questions are left to the initiative of ministers and the government, and the Chair can in no way help the hon. member to insist upon a reply.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, let me make it quite clear. I was not, I repeat not, asking the Chair to insist on an answer to a question being given.
