Mr. Speaker, the minister's imagination in terms of his contribution always amazes me.
1 want to speak about rentals because a prospect was held out for renters in this country. The forecast in the government's own position paper was equally bleak.
Rental investment will thus dry up in most markets and vacancy rates in most markets will approach zero by 1983.
A black market will develop with the phenomenon of "key money" becoming prevalent.
You know, Mr. Speaker, what key money is. It is payment. It is a black market arrangement by which people are able to get access to accommodation in spite of the lack of suitable rental accommodation there is in Canada. I am not talking about the Soviet Union or Moscow. I am talking about Canada where it is getting ever so difficult to get suitable rental accommodation for those who cannot afford their own private home accommodation. Again I quote from the minister's own departmental papers:
Tight markets will produce waiting lists for rental units and force doubling up with family and friends. We will witness a substantial regression in housing conditions following 35 years of gradual improvement.
Those were the forecasts the government, the Minister of Finance and certainly the minister responsible for housing knew well prior to the budget. Indeed, the minister responsible for housing put his seat on the line by saying if there was not help in the budget for the home owners of Canada, he would resign. That is an honourable position for the minister to take, a minister who is sincere and determined to help home owners in Canada, and I applaud the minister for taking that position-
But!

-but after the expectation about assistance in that budget was raised by the minister, the minister was clearly undercut by his cabinet colleagues.
As we are well aware, the budget upset the plans of home owners and renters across the nation. What is remarkable about the budgetary proposals is how they could be drawn up with so little regard for their practical application and probable repercussion. We have seen this demonstrated with respect to the myriad of issues which come up in the question period day after day. My colleagues have asked questions as to what the Minister of Finance meant by certain budgetary proposals. Why were certain other provisions not made? In this particular context, why have the home owners of Canada been let down so severely? The answer of the government was to provide 550 million this year either to guarantee to repay deferred interest up to $3,000 if a home owner has substantial equity or to pay all or part of the interest deferred to a maximum of $3,000 in cases where the home owner has little equity. This funding covers mortgages renewed between September 1, 1981, and November 12, 1982, a period which does not take into consideration the record high rates on renewals during this past summer. As a result, even though there are 920,000 home owners renewing their mortgages in the applicable period, a relatively small number of those will qualify, and all those home owners who had renewals during the summer are left high and dry.
What did the budget do for renters, Mr. Speaker? As the minister prophesied, unless something is done in terms of providing rental accommodation, the housing industry will be decimated by the budget. By tying the deduction of interest expense to investment income, the industry loses a major incentive to expand. The provision doing away with the deduction of soft costs for MURBs has the same effect. It makes for stagnation in the industry at a time of unprecedented demand and shortage of supply. The 15,000 units that the Minister of Finance promised will not begin to fill the gap that these tax measures opened. With a little incentive, private industry could have done the job itself. Perhaps, after having had to battle with his colleagues in cabinet the minister will now understand that the government has little regard for the private sector of the economy.
The net effect of the budget will probably be a reduction in housing starts. The MURB program has been cancelled. We should remember that it is a program that was responsible for the construction of some 25,000 rental units last year, which is
10,000	more than the 15,000 units the government expects will be built under the program provided for in Bill C-89. Meanwhile, the government will reduce its commitment to subsidizing social housing in 1982 from 30,000 to 25,000-a drop of 5,000.
I wanted to go into more detail on this, Mr. Speaker, but I am sorry that I do not have the time. The minister has been under attack from many sources. I should like him to know
February 23, 1982

that 1 sympathize with him because I believe he is trying to do a good job. However, he has a responsibility to Canadians to demonstrate that when he said he would resign if he were not able to deliver, he will take the honourable course and do so. If he is an honourable man, and I believe he is, then in the interests of Canadians and in order to get this government on the right course, he will tender his resignation in light of the abysmal failure of the budget to deal with the housing problems in the country.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to contribute to the debate on Bill C-89. This was intended to be a very important piece of legislation. It is one that home owners have been waiting for with some anticipation but it offers much too little much too late to those who have already lost their homes or have resigned themselves to losing their homes.
The very desperate situation that home owners and renters find themselves in today is the result of the government's refusal to change its high interest rate policy and its refusal to tackle the housing industry problem head on in a responsible and equitable way.
There is no question that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) who is responsible for housing, missed an excellent opportunity to bring in legislation that would deal with the housing and high mortgage rates in a meaningful way. Instead, he and his colleagues in cabinet, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) needlessly chose to raise the expectation of home owners about the kind of relief the government would offer. Those expectations soon turned to bitter disappointment. Even under very heavy pressure by members of the House and Canadians everywhere, the minister only responded by making several public statements to the effect that a major relief package was on the way if people would only hold on until the November 12 budget. By then, he said, Canadians would be offered relief. His colleagues thought that in this way the heat would be taken off the subject.
Just days before the budget was brought down, the minister denied that he had made any previous promises to the effect that the government had a comprehensive scheme in mind to help Canadians. There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that the aftermath of this was that the minister was heavily criticized in cabinet for supposedly giving budget secrets away.
The bill before us proves that the government's plans for relief for home owners, renters and the housing industry, should not be taken too seriously. It is very obvious that the government hopes to get away with paying token service to this ever-present problem by offering minor, short-term relief, all the while content to cross its fingers in the hope that inflation and interest rates will soon drop and that it can claim success.
When we look at the current problems facing the housing sector and the way the government has addressed them, it is clear that it is waiting for the storm to pass while refusing to deal with the problem itself.
Housing
There is no question that affordability and availability of houses in Canada are the two main areas where very serious problems have developed in the last few years.
In terms of availability of homes, it is quite clear that new housing starts are dropping far behind current demand and that this is resulting in increasing shortages. It has been estimated by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and by the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada that on average, Canada needs well over 200,000 new homes each year just to keep up with consumer demand. Yet, over the past four or five years, housing starts have consistently fallen far behind.
In 1977 we needed 256,000 units but 245,000 were constructed. The figures are worse each year. In 1978 we required
259,000	units but only 227,000 units were built. This trend continues today, Mr. Speaker. In 1981 we needed 265,000 units but only 170,000 units were produced. It is predicted that in 1982, housing starts will number about 135,000 while the actual need will be about 261,000 units. As you can readily see, Mr. Speaker, the situation is deteriorating very rapidly.
Availability in the rental or apartment sector is not much better. From the government's own Figures and predictions as revealed in the CMHC document leaked last fall, it is clear how serious the problem is. The government predicts that by 1983, we will have a zero vacancy rate right across the country. However, if current trends continue we could well reach that by next summer. The national vacancy rate fell from 2.8 per cent in 1980 to 1.2 per cent in October, 1981. In some metropolitan areas the vacancy rate already stands at zero per cent. It is evident from all this that the situation continues to deteriorate at a very rapid pace.
The government has estimated that about 90,000 rental units per year are needed to meet our rental requirements, yet it seems unable to assist in a meaningful way any rental construction, outside government assisted rental housing projects. At least this appears to be the case, given the government's continued support of a high interest rate policy and a budget filled with disincentives for private investment to move into rental construction.
An example of this disincentive is the cancellation of the multiple residential building program. By killing this plan it is estimated that 20,000 fewer units will be started this year.
In place of this very sensible program, the government introduced interest free loans of $7,500 for each of the 15,000 units to be built in various areas of the country. This program does not even begin to meet the strong demand for rental housing in Canada, and the leaked CMHC document admitted that the rental market is drying up very quickly. The MURB program served rental construction needs much better than the government's replacement, given the fact that its goal of
15,000	units does not come close to meeting current or future demands.
When we turn to affordability of housing, it is quite clear that the dream of owning a home is becoming a genuine

February 23, 1982
Housing
nightmare. In the last three months of 1981 the average cost of a home sold in Canada was $77,900. If we assume a 10 per cent down payment and, $1,000 in property taxes and accept the general principle that payments of principal, interest and taxes should not exceed 30 per cent of the gross income of a home owner, an annual family income of $44,500 is needed to purchase an average priced home. How many Canadians who face mortgage renewals make this amount of money? With prices so high, who can really afford to purchase a home today? Real estate agents tell us how depressed their business is because very few people can cope with the high asking prices for homes, to say nothing of the unreasonable and very high interest rates involved in assuming a mortgage.
Unfortunately, there is another great segment of our home owner population who have already purchased homes and are now at the mercy of high interest rates because they are required to renew their mortgages. Over the next two years approximately 1,200,000 families will find themselves in such an impossible situation. CMHC admitted that some 40,000 Canadians may well lose their homes because of continued high interest rates, yet the government refuses to extend any meaningful aid to home owners, no matter how many Canadians lose their homes or their life savings.
Removal of building subsidies in the rental industry is putting increased pressure upon monthly rental levels. The Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada estimated that removal of federal subsidies in terms of investor returns can only be replaced by rent increases of some 60 per cent or more. Because this situation is impractical and unrealistic, it is quite clear that potential investors are staying away from this area. Therefore, the government is killing this very important industry which it says it is trying to help with the bill. The result will be massive unemployment, not to mention a stagnant industry incapable of meeting necessary consumer demands.
I should like to take a brief look at what the government offers Canadians in this bill to show that their sense of outrage and criticism is completely justified. Canadian home owners, collectively, will not be better off because of the bill. To save face, the government will be extending some band-aid assistance to two groups of home owners facing mortgage renewals. The first group, estimated by CMHC to be about 12,500 in number, will receive a once-in-a-lifetime grant of some $3,000. This grant is designed for those people who have too little equity in their homes to support any interest deferral scheme. The second group, estimated to be about 37,500 in number, face monthly mortgage payments of over 30 per cent of their gross income. They will receive government guarantees of up to $3,000 which are designed to convince lenders to allow home owners to fend off some of the high interest rates. However, this scheme applies only to those home owners who renewed their mortgages between September 1, 1981 and November 12, 1982, and to those who pay over 30 per cent of their gross income on mortgage payments. The grant and loan plans will only help 50,000 people out of an estimated 920,000 home owners who renew their mortgages during the prescribed time. Of the 900,000 Canadians who will renew their mortgages, 100,000 face the very real possibility of losing their
homes, yet the government will only help directly 12,500 home owners with $3,000 grants. Canadians left in the cold face the bleak prospect of renewed mortgage rates of approximately 20 per cent or so. It is not something to which one looks forward.
Another disturbing aspect of the bill is that aid offered to home owners in a mortgage deferral program merely puts them deeper and deeper into debt. The leaked government document admitted that interest deferral schemes appeared unlikely to cure the problem faced by Canadians renewing their mortgages. In spite of the leaked CMHC document, the cabinet chose cosmetic relief. It is hoping that lending institutions will agree to provide interest free deferrals with the encouragement of guarantees.
As mentioned earlier in terms of assistance in the area of rental, the government announced a very feeble program to encourage construction of 15,000 rental units costing some $125 million in low vacancy areas. The program offers free loans of up to $7,500 per unit. What is really needed to protect Canadians from crippling mortgage interest rates and to prevent them from losing their homes is a mortgage interest and property tax credit similar to the one introduced by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) when he was minister of finance. If this program were in place today, home owners would enjoy tax credits of $1,125 for 1981 and $1,500 for 1982. The program would have made over $2 billion of relief available to home owners. At that time we offered $2.3 billion in relief, while the government only offered $50 million for this year.
Once again home owners who are on the short end of the stick when dealing with the government are those who insulated their homes with urea formaldehyde foam insulation on the advice and financial backing of the federal government. Anyone who is currently trying to sell or renew the mortgage on their homes with this insulation knows all about UFFI. Their homes are worthless and hazardous to the health and wellbeing of the occupants, yet it took the government over a year, after it banned the use of UFFI from the market, to bring in a relief program to help clean up a very messy situation which it created. The government is taking its sweet time to begin processing applications, obviously wanting Canadians to shoulder the financial burden themselves at a cost which can easily run into thousands of dollars per household. If the government had acted quicker, it would not be faced with so many angry Canadians, not to mention the problem of removing the foam. There is no question that the government has a responsibility to help remove UFFI because it pushed Canadians to use it. It is clear that the most common sense approach would be for the government to own up to its responsibility, to recognize a mistake was indeed made, to stop dragging its feet, and to pay full compensation to home owners involved in this government-sponsored mess.
I believe, as do most Canadians, that shelter is one of our basic rights. Everyone is or should be entitled to a home. However, while it may be a recognized right, we are slowly

losing our ability to obtain shelter. Yet the government has little or nothing to offer thousands of Canadians who are facing the immediate threat of losing their homes.
Bill C-89 hardly even addresses the deep financial problem facing home owners or the housing industry itself. The bill is totally inadequate. If the government had listened to Canadians and found out what they really need, we would have had a better financed more wide-ranging and comprehensive piece of legislation before us today. We can only hope the government will accept some of the amendments and change the bill before it passes the House. I will not hold my breath that such changes will take place. I have come to learn during the ten years that I have been a member of the House that the most uncommon thing to find on the other side is common sense. It is truly unfortunate and tragic that this place is just one more place where theory and theoretical ideas always take precedence over practical ideas which actually work better both in terms of application and in lower costs to the taxpayers in the long run. It is no wonder that our farmers and our producers are the most efficient people to be found anywhere in the world. They are practical people with little time for nonsensical theories and ideas that usually do not have a firm foundation to stand the test of practicality.
Whoever coined the expression that there is no experience like practical experience never spoke a truer word. It is too bad that many people who should know better chose to ignore these words of true wisdom.

As I stand here today, February 23, 1982, I stand with some sense of impending doom, and with a great deal of impending sadness. I look at Bill C-89, an act to amend the National Housing Act and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and I ask myself why am I standing here this evening debating a bill of this kind. As I reach out and look for the answer, 1 find that it is because this country is in crisis. But in a time of crisis, I would hope to see a piece of legislation that might help us overcome that crisis. When I look at Bill C-89, I do not see in this legislation any sense of real hope for average Canadians. I see once again a piece of legislation which is taking the time of the House because the government has decided to engage once more in a piece of public relations chicanery, another piece of public relations trickery.
When there is a problem in Canada and it is identifiable, the government is quick off the mark to say that it will solve the problem. That story lasts three, four or five days or for as much mileage as hon. members of the Liberal Party can get

If the Clark government had been allowed by the New Democratic Party, the Liberal Party west, to pass the legislation which was before the House in December, 1979, that legislation on mortgage deductibility for home owners in the budget presented by the hon. minister from Newfoundland, which has been judged by those who are experts in their society as the fairest budget in the decade of the 1980s and by the poorest segment of Canadian society-

As if that were not bad enough-because people pay their mortgages and municipal taxes from after tax income, that is the amount of money in pay cheques, the money that is used to make those payments-they elected a government full of deceit and trickery that has doubled the indirect taxes in this country. That extra $100 a month, Mr. Speaker, in indirect taxes coming out of your take-home pay, when added to the extra $408 a month because of high interest rates, comes to $508 a month which Canadians are paying extra. What are they getting for it? They are still in the same house, still driving the same car, using the same heater in their home. They get nothing extra for that, except for the privilege of paying taxes to the Liberal and New Democratic parties. They have the privilege of paying all that extra money to advance causes which are designed not to help Canadians, Mr. Speaker, but to bamboozle them. A $100 million for advertising. How much better would this country be if that money were given to Canadians to reduce their monthly mortgage payments!
One of the purposes of the December, 1979 budget was to reduce federal borrowing. Of what significance is that to Canadians? Well, when this government was elected, 19 cents out of every tax dollar went to pay interest on the public debt. This morning we discovered that two short years later 23 cents out of every tax dollar collected goes to pay interest on the public debt. An increase of almost 20 per cent, Mr. Speaker. That is what public debt is all about. It is spending money today so that your children and your grandchildren can pay for it. I looked at those figures this morning, and I found that interest on the public debt is getting very close to the sum total of all indirect taxes taken from Canadians in a year. It amounts to $200 per month per household to pay interest on the public debt. Instead of paying that against a mortgage, Canadians are forced to pay that to the bankers in Switzerland, in New York and Canada simply to pay interest on the public debt.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in case some of the Liberal backbenchers or some of the NDP think that is a good thing, there is something else to remember. There is a limited amount of money in the world and it is sold to people at a kind of auction based on interest rates. Every Canadian who has to go out and borrow money to buy a home or expand a small business has to go into that auction market and compete for the money. They can go and say, "If you will loan me that money, I will give you 16 per cent". But in the auction market somebody else says, "I will give you 16!/2". Someone else says, "I will give you 17", or it could be 1 IVi, 18, 18!A or 19 per cent. Then the bidding stops and you get the money for 19 per cent. And if you get that today, you are lucky. Well, do you know who was bidding against you? The federal government. They were out there trying to borrow the same money you are trying to borrow for your home. And they, through that auction market, are driving up the cost of money.
Now, here we have a piece of legislation which will affect very few Canadians but which bears a title that suggests it is a panacea, the help that Canadians need. It says, focus your eye on it, the government is doing something. They have already spent an unknown amount of money advertising this program before Parliament even dealt with it. They drew the attention of Canadians to the fact that this piece of legislation was here, and said it would help. But each day that advertising campaign was going on, each day we stand here and debate the bill, that same government is out there borrowing money and driving up interest rates, thereby causing Canadians to pay a higher amount of money to borrow than would be true had we had a government in the last decade with any sense of fiscal responsibility.
Mr. Speaker, if we were not today paying 23 cents out of every tax dollar to pay interest on borrowed money, we could increase by 50 per cent the amount of money we spend on hospital care, social services and old age pensions, all of which touch the hearts of most of the members who sit in this chamber. It is help to those who need it most. But instead we send money off to the bankers in other parts of the world, 23 cents out of every dollar, $16.5 billion in total.
Last fall this government asked Canadians to buy Canada savings bonds at 19'/2 per cent. And here we sit in this chamber tonight addressing ourselves to legislation which has been advertised with your tax dollars to distract your attention away from the fact that the primary reason that Canadians are losing sleep worrying about losing their homes, or in fact losing their homes, is this government's policies. Canadians are worried about what is going to happen in the next three or four months when their mortgages come up for renewal. Their health is suffering, the tension is there, but the advertising says: Do not worry, we will bail you out. When you have to increase the price of gasoline by $1.80 a gallon, you have no money left to pay the mortgage on your house. It is a very simple situation.
If you really want to make it relevant, the then finance minister from Newfoundland stood in the House and told Canadians that they had a choice as to whether or not to drive their cars. He said that we were going to raise the price of gasoline 18 cents a gallon, but if they did not drive their cars they would not have to put that 18 cents in the public till. However, because they had to heat their houses, he said there would not be any tax on home heating oil. He said we would put the tax where there is a choice as to whether to spend it, but there is no choice as to whether to heat your home, so we will not put a tax there.
The New Democratic Party, the Liberal Party west, joined with their partners across the way and said "That is not a good deal. We will kick you out, put the other guys in and increase taxes on home heating oil". They agreed to an indirect tax of $100 per month, and mortgage rates rising 8 per cent. They said now we will have equity. Do you know the purest form of equity, the easiest thing in the world to divide into equal shares? It is nothing.
If all of us cease to work and farmers cease to produce, we will come to a perfect state of equity. However, we value a
society where those who want a little more, such as a little better home, car and better food, are willing to work a little harder to get it, they produce.
If the million unemployed Canadians could find useful work to do, we would be a nation engaged in the production of wealth. The harder we work, the more we produce, the better our health care systems, pensions for our senior citizens and those with physical handicaps.
That is the kind of vision that this party had and has. The Liberals and the New Democratic Party decided that our desire to provide tax relief to those who have to pay municipal taxes and make mortgage payments was not fair. They said all Canadians should not get some tax relief for owning a piece of property, a home.
Tonight, two years later, we stand in the House with a piece of legislation that will provide increased indebtedness to a segment of our society that is already in debt over its head, not able to make mortgage payments on their homes. This government says it will provide some insurance which will allow these people to borrow more money to go further into debt to delay the day of reckoning for two or three years. This legislation encourages a poorer segment of society to go deeper into debt and to postpone the day of reckoning for two years.
I ask members opposite whether they wish that back in December 1979 they had put in place the proposed scheme which would have provided tax relief for municipal taxes and interest payments on the mortgages of all Canadians who own a home. I ask the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party whether they feel that if that legislation had passed there would be today more construction, more jobs, more production in the factories of Ontario and Quebec of stoves, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners and carpets, and whether the demands for unemployment insurance and other social payments of that kind would be down because a higher portion of our population would be working. I ask hon. members to consider that.
I stand here tonight to accuse the New Democratic Party of causing this situation. I do so tonight as a Member of Parliament from the city of Calgary with the certain knowledge that some 25 miles from my home the voters last week elected a separatist. They come from a part of this country where government policy, and government policy alone, has killed close to 50 per cent of the jobs in the exploration and service part of the oil industry. Government policy and government policy alone has decided to send the money to Mexico, Saudi Arabia, Venezuela and Libya instead of investing it in drilling rigs and in Canadians to drill for oil and gas, to refine and deliver. It is a region of the country where I was born and raised. It has some of the most generous people in the world. They are the kind of people who will give you the shirt off their back. The member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) earlier gave a list of the litany of claims by the current minister responsible for housing with regard to this matter. Therefore, I will not go into them now. I happen to know the minister well from our days together on council in metropolitan Toronto. Therefore, 1 knew exactly what he meant and I am sure he chose his words well when he said, in introducing this bill, "The bill before the House for second reading is a response to the serious difficulty which faces Canadians." I know that the minister chooses his words well. He did not say "a significant response" or "an important response" or "an effective response". He is honest enough to know that it is only "a response". We hear consistently throughout this debate that the mortgage assistance proposal is for $50 million and the multiple unit assistance proposal in the bill is for $350 million over two years. To most Canadians that may sound like a great deal of money. It is if it is viewed in absolute terms. Perhaps we should try to put the government's housing priorities into context. The government is to provide $50 million in an attempt to deal with the problems of 920,000 Canadians who will face mortgage renewals during the lifetime of this program; of whom 50,000 fewer will even get help, we are told. What does this $50 million represent? It represents what we gave to the Algerian government to build a monument. In other words, this government's housing priority is just as important as a 434 foot monument in Algeria.
The government intends to provide $350 million over two years, or $175 million per year, to help those in need of rental housing in Canada. This also sounds like a lot of money. During my lifetime, which is not that long, and for years before, the single greatest support has been shelter, not just for old age when people come to need it but for their sense of wellbeing and feeling of independence. In my city, the number of tenants has increased from 20 per cent to 60 per cent since the war. There is a very valid reason why we built a lot of rental housing. We built-incidentally, the government did not build, the private investors built it-the housing in response to the household formation change which we sometimes call, in demographic terms, the baby boom. At the same time that we were doing this, we built a great deal of ownership housing in Toronto because we could see the time coming when those born during the baby boom grew up to their present age. When the CMHC documents predicted the majority demand would be for ownership housing, we knew it was necessary to have a stock to serve that demand in Toronto as well as across Canada.
Today we face interest rates which make it impossible for that baby boom generation of Canadians who are on the verge of being able to achieve what they thought was their dream and that of their parents; to own their own home. We now face policies which have made it impossible for them to do that.
As a party we argued in the last election campaign that home ownership is so important to the nation and to Canadians that it is well past the time we understood that it is simply unjust to say that Canadians should have to pay municipal tax out of after-tax income. They ought to be able to deduct their municipal tax from their federal tax. It is well past the time for us to understand that it is unjust to say that once a person has bought his house he may, through the tax system, reborrow money to make other investments and be able to deduct the interest then but not, at the same time, be able to deduct the interest to buy the house in the first place. That was the tax equity which was represented by our party's mortgage tax credit plan.
The government finally, having said throughout the election campaign that it did not understand or did not accept that there was a tax equity argument, recognized in the November budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen)-if I can be cynical-the argument that there is a question of equity in tax treatment. Did the government consider bringing in the only sensible policy to correct that inequity and make it possible for people who cannot afford homes and who are faced with monstrous increases in their mortgage interest rates to deduct? No, and this is not really perhaps as widely understood as I would like it to be. The government's sense of equity was not to make it possible for people to deduct the interest
when they first get a home; the government made it impossible for anybody else to deduct interest. In other words, rather than creating an incentive to help people build homes and help people buy them, in the budget the government took away the right of other people to deduct interest for other investments.
It is fundamental to an understanding of the philosophy behind this pittance of a housing bill to understand that it is not separate from the context of the economic philosophy of the government opposite. There are several reasons why, for example, we have a vacancy shortage of the kind we do in rental housing. The most significant point is that the rental housing market, which is where people start in the system when they come out of school or form their first household while they build up some equity to buy a home, was killed by the government opposite. It was killed when the government opposite some years ago took away the incentive for small investors to invest directly in rental property. It used to be in Canada that if a person had a little extra money and wanted to buy or build a duplex or a little apartment building or if a person had a loss or the depreciation of a building created a loss, he could carry that in his personal income, and it was a stimulation for those who wanted to help support their old age by having a little building with three to four units or a couple of units. Let us look at how apartments were created originally in Canada. In Montreal, for instance, nearly 50 per cent of the apartments were created using that system. This government started there. It killed that right to deduct, and it has done so persistently throughout its economic policy. This government regards this as some kind of tax loophole. It killed the right to get tax relief if a person is willing to invest in his country.
They do not want you to own anything.

It shows up again here where, having promised relief to home owners in order to get votes in the last election, the government now comes along and says that the only people who will get any help from the government are those who have no equity left because the economic policies of the government have destroyed home values. I can refer to case after case in my riding in which house values have dropped 35 per cent or more in the last year, which means there will be no equity left. In such a case, if a person is now bankrupt in house value, he will get a grant from the government. If he has not yet made it to that point under this program, the proposal before us is that he be allowed to borrow what little he has left as an interest deferral so that the government can take it from him next year when the program expires.
The government tried this in relation to AHOP and ARP. The government has slowly but surely eroded the ability to own by taking away the incentives for people to invest in mortgages and by taking away the incentive for people to build affordable rental housing, and the litany goes on and on.
The scariest part of the budget is not this statement of budget policy on housing assistance. The scariest part is when this policy gets to its final logical conclusion. I refer to the policy of the last 25 years of changes to the National Housing
February 23, 1982

Act, changes to CMCH provisions and changes respecting who can invest in this country. The final change is on the tax expenditure side of the budget document. If Canadians will look, they will find a statement that, according to the mandarins in the Department of Finance, we can look forward to the day when Canadians will have rent imputed to them on houses they own. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) looks askance. He knows full well where this is in the document. If he has not read it yet, I find that difficult to believe. If he reads it, he will find the proposal to impute rent on an owned home one lives in and has paid for. That imputed rent would be added to taxable income.
It is called confiscation.

In other words, if the government cannot drive people out with interest rates, it will do so with tax burdens. To anyone who follows the history of the fiscal policy of the government in relation to housing the conclusion of this policy should come as no surprise. Its conclusion is in the statement on the tax expenditure side of the budget document because that is the direction in which we have been going all this time. There seems somehow to be no awareness on the part of hon. members opposite that housing expenditures have been the most important expenditures Canadians make. Housing expenditures form some 30 per cent of the consumer price index. They have formed anywhere from 6 per cent to 8 per cent-in good years-of our gross national product. They have also been the underpinning of much of our society's economy through all their spin-off effects. Every time a house is built, bricklayers are put to work, electricians are put to work and plumbers are put to work. People who build roads are put to work building roads to that house. People who build furniture are put to work to provide furniture for that house. People who make carpets are put to work to provide carpets for that house. People who make windows are put to work to make windows for that house. We do not need a policy which will result, as this policy confirms, in a drop in housing starts of 30 per cent in one year. Projections in the government's own documents are just crazy. Last year we were getting projections from CMHC, and now we are falling short of those projections. I suspect next year the results will be even below this year's projections from the CMHC, not just because there is a fundamental lack of investor confidence in the policies of this government-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Check the facts.

The minister responsible for housing says I should check the facts. I suggest that the minister responsible for housing check his back because he will find that the pride the people of Scarborough felt for him when he was mayor will not reward him with a return to this House.
Johnny one-time.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Check the facts.

The minister responsible for housing keeps yelling, "Check the facts". The facts are that the minister promised Canadians mortgage relief, not 50,000 of 920,000,
Housing
which is a pittance. If that is what he means by a fact, he should check his facts. I think the minister knows that full well.
He is just uncomfortable.

Let me refer again to the minister's comments, since he has interjected, because it will perhaps make the point as well as it can be made. The minister speaks of facts. This is the government's philosophy on rental accommodation: "The fact is that without government support the construction of rental accommodation in this country is simply not a viable business". That is true, Mr. Speaker, because of the policies of the government opposite over the last 15 or 20 years. It seems to permeate every policy that comes from the other side. There seems to be a sense that the only way to get the economy going again is through some form of government support. Yet that will drive the country into fiscal bankruptcy, if it has not already.
There seems to be a sense that the way to get a rental housing policy is to take away all incentive to invest and then to tell people to come cap in hand, and they will get a $7,500 interest free loan. That is what we have as a rental housing policy.
The argument goes like this, Mr. Speaker. Last year's policy, MURB, under which 25,000 units were built, is no good; that what we need is to get rid of that and instead have a policy that will build 15,000 units over two years through interest free loans. People are supposed to believe that that is a better and more productive policy than encouraging them to build through MURBs and all the other incentives that are now gone, such as the capital cost allowance, depreciation or write-offs into personal income. According to the Liberal government, none of that worked but in fact, Mr. Speaker, those policies built the houses that Canadians live in today.
People were operating at a profit, however. Some people paid lower rents than they do today. The market vacancy rate was 5 per cent or 6 per cent and, as a result, rents were held down. So the government got rid of all those things and created a system based on the belief that without government support the construction of rental accommodation is simply not a viable business in this country.
Why does the government believe that is a necessary policy, Mr. Speaker? The answer is quite simple. It is the same answer as that which was given by the government in the National Energy Program. In effect, the government says that we cannot afford to let private individuals in this country develop oil and gas. The government will do it. It will levy taxes and confiscate as well. This government does not believe that it can afford to let private individuals accomplish things in this country. That is evident in this bill and it is evident in the National Energy Program. I see the minister who is responsible for the Kent commission is in the House. This shows up in the policy that says that we cannot trust newspapers in this

February 23, 1982
Housing
country either, and that we had better have people interfere with them. This is the consistent view that runs through Liberal policy today.
All the budget does, through this bill and all the other programs, is to take the trend line of the last 12 years of Liberal management of the country and because the existing political leadership of the Liberal Party is not going to be here after the next election, one way or the other-either they will honour their promises to quit or we will beat them-they have decided not to wait 12 years but to accomplish everything in four. The only accomplishment of the budget is to accelerate the idea that there is some sort of free lunch and that Canadians will understand that and vote accordingly. It promotes the idea that the way to get a house in this country is to become broke. In that case, the government will offer assistance. That is the way people can get shelter they can afford-not because they go out and earn the money to make a downpayment. We believe that taxpayers ought to be able to deduct the borrowing cost of that asset from their taxes, because a house is the single asset that is a protection against inflation. No matter what happens in the rest of the world, every Canadian who owns a home and has paid off the mortgage knows that he or she is about as well protected from the ravages of inflation as is possible.
Apparently the government does not believe we can afford that; it does not believe that we can afford to have independent thinking Canadians, and so it proposes to take away the sense of security that comes from having made an investment in a home. The government wants to make everybody dependent.
1 do not say that lightly, Mr. Speaker. When 1 was outside politics it took me a long time to see the trend line emerge and to come to the realization that the socialism represented in the housing policies of the government is endemic to everything it does.
We must establish that this policy is not independent of the rest of the government's policies. On that score 1 should like to deal with some information which was available to the government in a document issued by CMHC planners in July, 1981, entitled "The Demographic Future: Impacts on the Demand for Housing in Canada, 1981-2001." It was produced by Philip W. Brown of Market Forecasts and Analysis Division, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and was prepared for a symposium held at the University of British Columbia. The document laid out very clearly what was going to happen to housing trends in the country. It forecast that the major problem of 1980s and 1990s will almost certainly be the rental market.
That should not come as a surprise to those of us who follow this issue in the urban centres of this country, Mr. Speaker. Did we see stimulus through MURBs or stimulus for people who would build any form of rental housing? We did not. What we got was an argument from the government that it believed that 15,000 units of accommodation provided by the private sector over two years is all the government help that is
needed. We see an indication that the social housing side, which 1 admit is important, is more important to the government than simply getting people to invest in housing in this country.
The author makes the following point about the expectations of the baby boom generation. Members of that generation are now at the age when they are just about to buy a house, but he points out that this will not be possible for them. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the suggestion in the budget that a whole generation of Canadians should not be able to afford a home was already known to the minister and to Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. He suggests that there is more here than a simple failure to understand the rest of the world; that there is in fact a cynical attempt to prevent people from owning homes. On page 25 there appears the statement, "The whole question of expectation levels, for example, is critical". In the last paragraph he writes:
Realization that erosion of expectations is imminent or threatened may result in a search for further alternatives to curtail household expenditures besides the usual steps to increase income.
He goes on to indicate that the only solution for those who may want to own a home in this country may be to resort to some form of co-operative housing.
I appreciate that my time is about up, Mr. Speaker, but I want to say that if the only answer to the problem in this country is co-operative housing, if we have seen the end of the private home in this country, then I for one fear greatly about what will happen to my country.
Hear, hear!

ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-(A) INQUIRY RESPECTING INVESTIGATION OF CONVICTED MURDERER CLIFFORD OLSON; (B) STATEMENT MADE BY PROSECUTOR

["The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly, this House stands adjourned until two o'clock tomorrow afternoon.\nAt 10.27 p.m. the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.", 'Wednesday, February 24, 1982']

Mr. Speaker, last Friday I rose in the House to ask some questions of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) regarding the last four days of July, the activities of Clifford Olson and the manner in which the RCMP handled that particular problem. I do not like to ask those kinds of questions. I have a great deal of admiration for the RCMP. I admire its work and I have total confidence in it, yet it appears something has gone wrong in the handling of the affairs of Clifford Olson. The fact that the government is keeping a lid on this is keeping line officers of the RCMP from doing their very best and maintaining their reputation.
February 23, 1982

1 should like to cite one simple example. A resident of an Edmonton suburb came to me a year ago and told me about an event in that community. Some young people were having a private party. In the midst of it, a gang of 60 or more young people came from the city of Edmonton to disrupt that very quiet and peaceful party. The parents then called on the RCMP in the community to come and take care of the disturbance. Two constables came out, handled the situation with dispatch and great efficiency, quelled the uprising if it can be called that, and the parents were supremely happy. The next or the following day the staff sergeant of the detachment wanted to discipline the two constables because they had not quite followed the book in the way they handled the affair.
This is what bothers me. It seems the staff sergeant was much more concerned about public image, public reputation and fear that public questions might be asked and, therefore, wanted to discipline the officers rather than commend them. It seems that in the Edmonton case the staff sergeant, middle management, wanted success to look life failure, and in the Olson case it looks to me like middle and upper management of the RCMP wanted failure to look like success. In both cases I believe the officers have done their work and have done it well, but somewhere in the Olson case, upper and middle management have made a series of errors and have frustrated the work of line officers. We need to know what has gone wrong in the decision-making level of the RCMP in this particular case.
Let me cite the sequence. On July 27 Burnaby RCMP were briefed by one of the officers on Olson as a prime suspect. He outlined the 92 convictions and the kinds of convictions which comprised the career of Clifford Olson. On the same day Surrey RCMP issued a warrant for Olson on a charge of indecent assault, and the police were commanded to arrest him forthwith. On July 28, the next day, eight cars of officers were involved in apprehending Olson and taking him into custody. Eight cars of officers were involved; I presume that would be 16 officers. On July 29 Olson walked out of jail in Surrey; he walked out of custody and surveillance of him was dropped. In the process the serious crimes division of the RCMP indicated that it wanted the warrant "taken care of', whatever that means.
On July 30, the following day, Olson spent the best part of the morning in a coffee shop with some RCMP officers discussing the offences of other criminals; there was a warrant outstanding on him but he was not arrested. On July 31 the special "O" unit of the RCMP asked for surveillance again. In the meantime, Olson had killed his eleventh and, presumably, his final victim. Again on July 31, the same day as the special "O" unit asked for surveillance to be dropped, the prosecutor asked that the "warrant be vacated". On the one hand the special unit wants surveillance, on the other hand there is an application to vacate the warrant.
There are some serious questions, and 1 want to enumerate them in the two or three minutes I have left. First, why was the
Adjournment Debate
warrant issued four days previously and then vacated? In four days it was vacated. Second, why did the prosecutor on July 31 say, "I didn't get feedback from the police."? Four days previously Olson had been named a prime suspect and 16 officers were involved in his apprehension. Third, why could officers spend all morning with him and not arrest him when they knew there was a warrant out for him? Fourth, who authorized Olson's release?
Why will the assistant commissioner Don Wilson and the Solicitor General not answer these questions? Why do they choose to stonewall? I can say with assurance that these questions will not go away. They will be answered one way or the other. The Solicitor General says he wants to maintain the integrity of the RCMP. The only way he can do that is to be open and honest, and free them from the pall of universal guilt they are sharing because several people have apparently made some wrong decisions. The Solicitor General has not come clean on that.
I am again asking for a full and independent inquiry into the affairs of this case.
[ Translation]

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to indicate that I agree with my colleague when he says that he admires the RCMP. I believe that most Canadians appreciate the job they do. I would suggest to the hon. member who intends to repeat the same questions again that, rather than making political mileage out of tragic events which occurred in British Columbia, he should tell the population that the administration of justice is exclusively a provincial matter, and I would also advise him to provide accurate information.

On February 19 last, the hon. member asked questions of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) pertaining to details of the police investigation of Clifford Olson. The Solicitor General then answered that the attorney general of British Columbia had answered these questions previously. As well, they were the subject of a press conference held by the RCMP in Vancouver. It is always better to have the facts of an investigation explained by those close to the scene and this has been done in this case. Answers have been provided and can continue to be provided by those who were involved in the investigation, namely, the local RCMP and the attorney general of British Columbia.
With respect to the hon. member's second question, the Solicitor General has asked the attorney general of British Columbia if he was satisfied with the police conduct of the investigation, and I am sure that if the prosecutor had not been properly briefed by the police, the attorney general of British Columbia would have mentioned this to the minister. He did not do so.

February 23, 1982
Adjournment Debate
EXPORT DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-(A) CONSTRUCTION OF MONUMENT IN ALGERIA; (B) USE OF CORPORATION RESOURCES

Mr. Speaker, the question I raised on February 11, 1982, regarding the appropriateness of Canadians financing the construction of a large edifice for Algeria, to the extent of $50 million, is fairly complex. My colleague across the aisle will tonight probably be attempting, as well as he can, to justify this particular course of action. 1 will leave that to him. Obviously there are certain benefits for Canadian business, shipping and other elements, that will to some extent justify, at least in the minds of the government, this rather unusual exercise on behalf of the Export Development Corporation. On the other hand, 1 feel there are higher and better priorities for the Export Development Corporation. The answer given by the minister on February 11, reads as follows:
Madam Speaker, this is not at all unusual. It is an ordinary export financing operation of the EDC.
That, Mr. Speaker, is manifestly stretching the point.
1 do not know how many other projects we are financing around the world which involve building a monument to a revolution in a country where the money could probably be very much better utilized for some other purpose. 1 do not know if there are any other countries building similar monuments. If there are, perhaps the minister's answer may be factually correct, but I would sure like to hear about them tonight.
In addition, as a matter of principle, I and many other Canadians would like to know the reason for the secrecy surrounding the interest and repayment terms. I suppose it will be contended, as it often is, that commercial necessity or confidentiality is the criterion. In my view, Sir, this is utter nonsense. Canadian taxpayers are entitled to know what their government agencies are doing, on what basis and for what purpose. But this government, Sir, has never believed that, and it is unrealistic for me, I suppose, to expect any answer on that score tonight.
My feelings are not unique, and I am getting quite a bit of mail on this matter. One letter which came in today from a Toronto businessman pretty well sums up the feelings, I think, of many Canadians when they read about these subsidized projects involving gas projects in the Soviet Union, which are of doubtful strategic value and cost Canadian taxpayers millions of dollars in subsidies, or Algerian monuments. This letter is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan). It bears a fairly recent postmark, although we cannot expect too much from the mail these days. As you know, Mr. Speaker, it costs 30 cents to mail a letter, which works out to about one cent a day in delivery time. The letter reads:
The attached newspaper item was published on the same page as the obituaries and rightly so, as it represents what is surely the death of reason! May I, as a poor slob of a taxpayer-
And this is the way the man feels:
-please have explained to me, how $46,700,000 can be justified to the benefit of my fellow Canadians, with the exception of Messrs Lavalin International of Montreal, Quebec.
I should say at this point, Mr. Speaker, that company is only doing its job as an aggressive Canadian corporation. I have no quarrel with it; the priorities are what bother me. The letter goes on to say:
1 am told that we (the public) must use restraint and conserve our monetary resources, and not buy unnecessary things like homes, automobiles, appliances, or anything that might improve the employment problems, directly involved. And yet you have authorized the outrageous amount to build a bloody monument-
I know that you don't give a damn what people like me think, but perhaps you could make an exception in this case and explain to me the following:
Now, this is a Canadian taxpayer and businessman speaking. He says:
If you feel that you have to waste these funds anyway, why not on a hospital, school, factory, or something useful.
My sentiments, exactly, Sir. He goes on:
What are the terms of the loan and what interest?
Do you really think we will get an answer to that? I do not think so, Sir. It goes on:
How many Canadians are going to benefit from the actual construction and from the effects, after the ... thing is finished.
In fairness, there are jobs being created there now. As I said, it is not all on the down side. However, that is a good point. Next June, when this accelerated project is over and the people of Algeria have their monument, what lasting good is it going to do for the people of either Canada or Algeria? The letter goes on:
How much (dollars) business did Canada do with Algeria in 1981, that the Algerians actually paid for, and 1 don't mean a Third World grant.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, there is a real problem, as far as our taxpayers are concerned, in using our Export Development Corporation to finance a project like this. Despite Canadian content, despite the good things that may be said in terms of making a breakthrough in Algeria with Canadian technology-if this occurs it is not all on the down side-the problem is compounded greatly, Sir, by the persistent lack of information and co-operation which agencies like the Export Development Corporation put in the way of taxpayers like this man who wants to know what the heck is going on. Many Canadians do not mind helping the Third World, either through an Export Development Corporation loan, or through CIDA, as far as that goes. That is an entirely different matter, but even in this regard we cannot find out what is going on.
As members opposite may know, we are presently negotiating to spend about $200 million in Trinidad and Tobago to construct two airports and a prison. I do not know whether this is a good thing, but it is a sure thing. We could certainly use money like that, and like the money provided through the EDC alone to Algeria, here in Canada.
February 23, 1982

I have recently written to the minister in charge of economic development about industries in Nova Scotia which have a high export potential, such as Sydney Steel and Hawker Siddeley Canada Ltd. in Trenton, Nova Scotia. We would love to see the Canadian Export Development Corporation financing steel rails or railway rolling stock which would be useful to Third World countries and would protect the jobs of thousands of Nova Scotians.
I see that my allotted time has just about expired.
However, instead of that, we have a priority, through a very potentially useful export development agency which is utilized by a Third World country, to build a monument, financed to some extent by the people of Canada on a subsidized basis. We do not know the terms. We do not know, in fact, if it is a soft loan or if we will ever get it back. I am sure none of us in this chamber, including my hon. friend opposite who will be very ably defending this transaction, really believes that this was the purpose for which the Export Development Corporation was founded or that this is the highest and best use of this kind of credit. Much as this may appeal to the nationalistic and historical tendencies of the Algerian people who want to build a monument, I think there are quite a few other things they could build first.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Celine Hervieux-Payette (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to give some clarification to the hon. member.

In December, the Export Development Corporation agreed to provide $47.6 million or 85 per cent of the value of a contract awarded to Lavalin International for the first phase of an important project in Algeria. This contract includes design, engineering, services, construction management and the provision of Canadian goods and services. All this, Mr. Speaker, means providing 3,000 man-years of employment in Canada.
This project, the main purpose of which is to commemorate the twentieth anniversary of Algerian independence, includes the building of facilities and public works. In fact, the monument to the martyrs will be built within the context of a vast development project including the building of public facilities such as museums, shops, etc. The financing provided for this project is part of a credit margin of $1.2 billion agreed upon in 1980 between the Export Development Corporation and the Algerian Development Bank. Therefore, the financing of this project is normal for the provision of Canadian goods and services and is similar to the type of export financing granted by the EDC to other countries.
This is neither a subsidy nor a loan, but straight financing. Moreover, there are ongoing trade negotiations between the Lavalin Corporation and the Algerian authorities regarding another contract for the provision of goods and services within the same project. However, it would not be proper at this time to comment on the terms and conditions of this potential contract as long as the negotiations with the foreign customers
Adjournment Debate
have not been completed. Hon. members surely realize that in this case, the client's motive and sensitivity will not allow us to discuss this matter as long as the trade and financial arrangements have not been finalized. All further arrangements would be subject to the same terms and conditions as the present contract. However, consistent with a long-established policy in the area of export financing, interest rates are never made public, as they are negotiated in each case and their disclosure could jeopardize future transactions. I repeat that this is not a new approach which would apply to Algeria alone, but is the current policy of the EDC.

subtopic: AIR SAFETY-MANAGEMENT OF AVIATION SAFETY BOARD
AIR SAFETY-MANAGEMENT OF AVIATION SAFETY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I would like to pursue, in more depth, a question I raised today in the House. Unfortunately, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) was not available to comment on it. This was unfortunate because it concerned the third and final report of Justice Dubin on air safety in Canada and the combination of roughly 247 extremely well-founded recommendations for improving the safety of the entire air transportation system in this country.
Within that report there were three key aspects to implementing the recommendations Justice Dubin laid out. Those three key areas involve reorganization of the department, a legislative process that would give force and effect to the recommendations that were proposed and, finally, a financial commitment that would see those recommendations put in place in an effective manner.
The first question related to the matter of reorganizing the department. What is basically needed here is a concept paper or a background paper that would allow the individuals in this country involved in the system to understand where the government is going and to learn of its commitment. There is also a question involving the Canadian aviation safety board, its structure and operation, its relationship to other federal departments and provincial authorities such as coroners and the Workmen's Compensation Board which, because of reneging on the federal air transport administration, has wound up involved in the air safety business. There is also the question regarding the enforcement branch, its structure and operation.
Canada has had some fairly effective laws and committed individuals in the field. Because of problems and a lack of resolve in the whole area of enforcement, our system has collapsed at least to the point where the government of the day and the population are seriously concerned about air safety and the need to strengthen this enforcement arm. Had enforcement been more rigourous at the senior levels, we would probably not have this problem before us in its present scope.
A very important part of reorganization is the placing of search and rescue under the aegis of the Ministry of Transport.

February 23, 1982
Adjournment Debate
This is a very significant and important role. We need information, whether it is a concept paper or some kind of a background information, to know where the government is going in this direction and to learn of its commitment.
The second point the government might consider in the development of such a paper is the idea of explaining the legislative process which will be used to implement the recommendations to the people of Canada. The group task force on the Aeronautics Act has been struggling valiantly for years with this project. I suppose we will not see the fruits of their labours in the term of this Parliament. If we wait too long for a finished piece of legislation which encompasses everything in the Dubin report, we will probably never have it during this Parliament. This will pass on as a temporary embarrassment, and the government will forget about it.
On the other hand, it would be interesting to learn from the government what its intentions are in terms of providing us with the legislative program to implement the Canadian aviation safety board, the delegation of authority to the enforcement branch, the strengthening of airworthiness and personnel licensing.
My last request, and this would be extremely interesting, is to have the government's intentions outlined in the form of the background paper on the financial commitment that will be required to put this entire report and its recommendations, which the minister has already endorsed, in place. This will all require capital investment for airport improvements, navigation system improvements, communications, and financial commitments for radar.
The parliamentary secretary today again announced, and this has been announced I do not know how many times, the $217 million ramp program. I do not know how many times we have heard about this. We know the program will be phased in over ten years. There are some very serious questions about it. We need information, information that should be made public. The program should be accelerated, and it must ensure that the equipment is the top state of the art. We need a concept or white paper to tell us what are the intentions of the government. Financial commitments for training programs are extremely important. Who will bear this burden? Will it be the taxpayers? What will be the effect on small carriers? How will these costs be passed through to private aviation? These are all questions in terms of the financial commitment of the government on which we need some information.
There has to be a solid commitment on the part of the government; a sharing of information; a commitment of
financial and human resources to put the recommendations of the Dubin report in place. I hope the parliamentary secretary will be able to shed some light on these matters.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR SAFETY-MANAGEMENT OF AVIATION SAFETY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the tabling of the first volume of the Commission of Inquiry on Aviation Safety, the minister has made a continual effort to respond quickly and positively to Judge Dubin's recommendations.
Legislation to establish a Canadian aviation safety board, as recommended in Volume I of the report, is well advanced and should be ready for tabling in Parliament late this spring. As recently announced, a newly published compliance and enforcement manual gives effect to recommendations in Volume II, that a more vigorous enforcement policy be adopted. Amendments to the Aeronautics Act, also recommended in Volume II, are being developed and a bill will be brought before Parliament at the earliest practicable date.
The third and final volume is highly technical and requires some study. However, the minister will give it high priority and the hon. member should have confidence that the minister will respond to it in the same positive manner as he responded to the previous volumes.
Action has already been taken in some areas identified by Judge Dubin in Volume III. For example, emergency locator transmitters, conforming to new standards, will again become mandatory as of April 1, 1982. As for upgrading radar, tendering for a new radar system, expected to cost over $217 million, will begin in a few weeks.
On previous occasions the hon. member has called for the removal of the senior management of the air administration. The minister has asked for co-operation and open-mindedness on the part of his officials in responding to Judge Dubin's fundamental reassessment of the civil aviation system. The positive action taken on Volumes I and II demonstrates that he has so far received it. The minister fully expects that he will continue to enjoy the support of his officials in promoting and maintaining the safest possible civil aviation system.
